name: Jade Ito

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: Thank you for talking with me, Jade. I'm a field researcher with the Work Futures Panel, an independent research group with no ties to AI companies, employers, unions or government. It's all confidential, so you can tell me what you'd say in public and what you really think. Could you describe a normal working day?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I'm at the Bauer farm at six, they've got about ninety milking goats, some hay ground and a vegetable patch for the farm shop. I help with milking, clean the parlour, feed the kids, the baby goats I mean, and then three days a week I'm in the dairy with Mrs Bauer learning to make the soft cheese. I'm still the beginner, she checks every batch I make.

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: How did you come to this, and what's hard?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I was a hairdresser for thirty-five years, renting a chair in town, and when Ken got the caretaker job at the church and school out here, I fancied a change at 56. What's hard is the pay, it's the bottom rate, and the early starts when my wrists ache. Ken's wage is small too, so we've got less than a month saved, but we've got the cottage that comes with his job.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The first picture is called AI Plateau. Picture this. AI turns out to be mostly hype. It automates some routine tasks and saves a bit of time here and there, but nothing radical changes. Jobs, pay and prices carry on much as they would have anyway. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say I'm not surprised, but I'd keep using it anyway, it helps me. At church I'd tell the ladies it's just a clever notebook. Online I'd say the hype people should have been quieter.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: For me nothing changes, which means the bottom rate and a thin cushion. The goat farm is doing fine, the shop sells everything Mrs Bauer makes. My worry is what happens if Ken's job goes, because the cottage goes with it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd keep learning the cheese with Mrs Bauer and use the AI every evening to look up what went wrong with a batch. I'd start doing haircuts in the kitchen on Saturdays again, maybe five a week, for about seventy-five pounds. I cut hair for thirty-five years, so I know that people will pay more for something made by a person who remembers their name.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Content with the work, a bit watchful about money and the cottage.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What do you use AI for now, exactly?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I keep a goat health diary on it, which goat had a limp, which one's off her feed, and I ask it why my cheese curd went rubbery. I also use it to write the church newsletter, which used to take me a whole evening. Ken calls it my assistant.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Why would Ken's job be at risk?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: The church council is always talking about money, and the school might merge with the one in the next village. If either happens, Ken's job shrinks, and the cottage is tied to it. That's the worry under everything.

say: I'd say I'm **not surprised** but would keep using AI because it **helps me**.
I'd tell the church ladies it's just a **clever notebook**.
think: The goat farm is **doing fine**, so my job feels safe.
If Ken's job goes, our **tied cottage** goes with it.
do: Use AI every evening to **fix cheese batches** and keep the goat diary.
Do **Saturday haircuts** in the kitchen, about seventy-five a week.
feel: **Content** with the work but **watchful** about money and the cottage.
S0.quote: I cut hair for thirty-five years, so I know that people will pay more for something made by a person who remembers their name.
fieldNote: She already uses AI **daily** for goat records, cheese and the **church newsletter**.
Her hidden risk is the **tied cottage**, which depends on her husband's job.
She restarts **haircutting** as a quick, real side income.

steps.text: Use AI each evening to diagnose cheese batches and log goat health
Cut hair in the kitchen on Saturdays, about five clients

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The second picture is called Steady Disruption. Now picture this. AI brings strong change, but not a revolution. Over the next few years it takes over many thinking tasks in many jobs: writing, checking, planning, buying, booking, coding and answering customers. Robots spread into hands-on work more slowly. Some jobs shrink, new ones appear, and lots of people have to change how they work. Most people still have work, and there is some time to adjust. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say it's good news for small family businesses if they use it wisely. At church I'd say hard-working people adapt, they always have. Online I'd share how I use it on the farm, to show older people it's not scary.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: For me it's mostly a help. I'd happily let a computer do the Bauers' (her bosses') goat records, because I'd rather spend that hour with the goats than with the spreadsheet. The robots coming slowly means my hands still matter, especially in the dairy.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd set up a proper AI system for the Bauers' herd records and shop orders, I'd offer to do it on my own time. I'd ask Mrs Bauer if I could make a small batch of my own cheese under the farm's name and sell it online with a story about it being handmade. I'd keep the haircuts going too.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Hopeful and busy. A bit nervous about asking Mrs Bauer for anything.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Why nervous about Mrs Bauer?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Because I'm the beginner and it's her recipe and her name. I'd want to ask properly, maybe offer her most of the money from the first batches. Respect matters in a family business.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Who'd lose out in this picture, do you think?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: The girls at the call centre in town, and the people doing office paperwork at the council. It's sad, but the market moves, and they'll have to move with it. I did, at 56.

say: I'd call it **good news** for small family businesses that use it wisely.
I'd share how I use AI to show **older people** it's not scary.
think: A computer doing the **goat records** frees me for the goats themselves.
Robots coming **slowly** means my hands still matter in the dairy.
do: Set up an AI system for the Bauers' **herd records** and shop orders.
Ask Mrs Bauer to let me sell my own **handmade cheese** online.
feel: **Hopeful** and busy, a bit **nervous** about asking Mrs Bauer.
S1.quote: I'd happily let a computer do the Bauers' (her bosses') goat records, because I'd rather spend that hour with the goats than with the spreadsheet.
fieldNote: She sees thinking AI as **freeing time** for her hands-on work, not threatening it.
She frames change as **personal responsibility**, citing her own move at 56.
She treats the owner with **careful respect**, offering her most of the early profit.

steps.text: Set up AI for the Bauers' herd records and shop orders
Sell a small handmade cheese line online under the farm's name

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The third picture is called AGI by 2028. Next one. The singularity hits fast. Within 2 years, by 2028, there is full AGI: artificial general intelligence, meaning AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do, as well or better, and cheaper. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2031. It arrives before most companies, governments and families have time to prepare. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say it's a test, and families and churches will have to carry each other through it. I wouldn't ask the government for much, they'd only get in the way. Online I'd keep sharing what's working for small producers.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: The thinking AI in 2028 I'd use straight away, I already do. When the robots can milk goats, the only thing left that's mine is the cheese with my name on the label. The robots in 2031 hit me at 63, and goat parlours aren't so different from cow parlours, which already have robots.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: In the first year I'd build my own cheese label properly, with Mrs Bauer's blessing, and get it into two farm shops and the market. I'd learn to run the milking robot when it comes, so I'm the one who looks after it. We'd cut back hard too, no holiday, the cheapest phone plans, to save for 2031.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Anxious, I won't pretend otherwise. But I'd be too busy to sit with it for long.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you tell your daughter Mei?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Mei's a dental nurse, so the robots are a while off for her, but the booking and the forms will go. I'd tell her to be the nurse patients ask for by name. That's what kept my chair full for thirty-five years.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Is handmade cheese really enough to live on?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Not on its own, no. With the haircuts and whatever the Bauers keep me for, maybe. I'd be honest and say I don't know, but I'd rather try than wait.

say: I'd call it **a test** that families and churches will carry each other through.
I'd keep the **government** out and share what works for **small producers**.
think: Robots that can **milk goats** leave only my named cheese as mine.
Robots in **2031** hit me at 63, since parlours already use them.
do: Build my own **cheese label** and get it into two farm shops.
Learn to run the **milking robot** so I'm the one who looks after it.
Cut the **holiday** and phone plans to save for 2031.
feel: **Anxious**, but **too busy** to sit with it long.
S2.quote: When the robots can milk goats, the only thing left that's mine is the cheese with my name on the label.
fieldNote: She sees the **three-year gap** as time to build her own named product before robots arrive.
She expects thinking AI to help her, but **robot milking** to take the core of her job.
She admits she **doesn't know** whether cheese and haircuts can carry them.

steps.text: Launch my own cheese label in two farm shops and the market
Learn to run and clean the goat milking robot
Skip the holiday and move to the cheapest phone plans

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The fourth picture is called AGI by 2031. Now the same thing, a bit slower. Full AGI arrives within 5 years, by 2031: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2034. There are a few years to see it coming, but it's still fast. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say five years is a blessing, enough to build something. At church I'd tell people to start now, not complain later. Online I'd keep showing what a small farm can do.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Robots around 2034 means I'd be 66, so I'd have a few years in the dairy before they arrive. That's time to get the cheese known. The worry is still Ken's job and the cottage, which has nothing to do with AI.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Five years is enough time to build a cheese that people drive out to the farm for. I'd buy a small second-hand cheese press, a few hundred pounds, with the haircut money over a year. I'd use AI to plan the batches, the labels and the orders, and I'd keep learning the cheese with Mrs Bauer.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Uneasy about the cottage, excited about the cheese.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: A few hundred pounds is a lot with under a month saved. Why risk it?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Because the press lets me make hard cheese, which keeps, and keeping is what makes money in a small dairy. I'd only buy it after a year of haircut money, not on credit. I don't borrow, my mother never did.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And if Ken's job went?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Then we'd have to find a rented place, and the cheese money would have to cover rent. I'd pray it doesn't come to that. Our son Hiro has said we can stay with him for a while, but he's got his own family.

say: I'd call five years a **blessing** with time to **build** something.
I'd tell people at church to **start now**, not complain later.
think: Robots in **2034** give me a few years to get the **cheese known**.
The cottage tied to **Ken's job** stays the bigger worry.
do: Buy a **second-hand cheese press** with a year of haircut money.
Use AI to plan **batches**, labels and orders.
feel: **Uneasy** about the cottage, **excited** about the cheese.
S3.quote: Five years is enough time to build a cheese that people drive out to the farm for.
fieldNote: Five years lets her **invest** carefully, paying cash rather than borrowing.
Her value of **not borrowing** comes from her mother.
The **tied cottage** stays her largest risk, unrelated to AI.

steps.text: Buy a second-hand cheese press with haircut savings
Plan cheese batches, labels and orders with AI
Get my own hard cheese sold at farm shops

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The fifth and last picture is called AGI by 2036. Last one. Full AGI arrives within 10 years, by 2036: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2039. It's the same end point, but there's about a decade to prepare, change careers and make plans. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say ten years is generous, and the Lord gives us time for a reason. At church I'd say teach the young ones a craft. I'd keep sharing my cheese posts online.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Robots in 2039 means I'm 71 and finished in the dairy, so my work is safe. The thinking AI I'd keep using, it makes me better at the cheese. My money worries stay, the thin cushion and Ken's tied cottage.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd keep going at the Bauers' and keep using AI every day. With ten years' warning, I'd spend the money teaching my granddaughter to make cheese, not on a pension I'll barely see. Rosa's twelve and she already loves the dairy.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Mostly calm, a little uneasy about the cottage.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Why teach Rosa rather than save?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Because the saving I can do is tiny, and a skill is something she keeps. If she can make good cheese by hand, people will buy it whatever the robots do. That's an inheritance I can actually give.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would your plans change at all with ten years?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Only that I'd go slower with the cheese label, build it properly. No rush. The goats aren't going anywhere.

say: I'd call ten years **generous** and say the young should learn **a craft**.
I'd keep sharing my **cheese posts** online.
think: Robots in **2039** come after I'm 71, so my dairy work is **safe**.
The **thin cushion** and Ken's tied cottage still worry me.
do: Keep working at the Bauers' using **AI every day**.
Teach my granddaughter Rosa to make **cheese by hand**.
Build my own cheese label **slowly** over the decade.
feel: Mostly **calm**, a little **uneasy** about the cottage.
S4.quote: With ten years' warning, I'd spend the money teaching my granddaughter to make cheese, not on a pension I'll barely see.
fieldNote: With a decade, the robots pass her by, but **housing** tied to Ken's job keeps her uneasy.
She sees a **skill** as the inheritance she can give, not money.
She would slow the cheese label and **build it properly**.

steps.text: Keep milking and making cheese at the Bauers'
Use AI daily for goat records and cheese batches
Teach granddaughter Rosa to make cheese by hand

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Of the five pictures, which one worries you most, and what would actually help you if it happened?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: AGI by 2028, because the milking robots would reach the goats when I'm 63, before my cheese has a name. What would help is farm shops and markets that make room for small local makers, and fewer forms for selling food from a small dairy.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Is there anything I didn't ask that I should have?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: Ask about faith. People think it makes you afraid of new things, but not me. God gave me hands and a head, and I'd be ungrateful not to use both, robots or no robots.

headlineQuote: God gave me hands and a head, and I'd be ungrateful not to use both, robots or no robots.
portrait: Jade is 58, a former **hairdresser** now learning goat milking and cheese on the Bauers' farm.
She and Ken, a church and school caretaker, live in a **tied cottage** with under a month saved.
She uses **AI daily** for goat records, cheese fixes and the church newsletter.
Her faith and **self-reliance** shape her: she prefers family and church to government, and won't borrow.
Fast robots make her **anxious**, while slower pictures leave her uneasy, mostly about the cottage.
biggestWorry: **AGI by 2028**, with milking robots arriving before her cheese has a name.
whatWouldHelp: Room in **farm shops** and markets for small local makers.
Fewer **forms** for selling food from a small dairy.
